en: [15a] A king who practices unrighteousness and injustice is generally praised by his dependents; therefore, with great difficulty, he discerns what is appropriate from what is inappropriate.
Even another person, whoever they may be, finds it difficult to speak that which is appropriate yet unpleasant.
How much more so, O King Mahābhūma, since I am but a mendicant?
Out of affection for you alone, and out of compassion for the world,
I alone speak to you what is beneficial, though it be very unpleasant.

"The disciple should be addressed at the proper time with words that are true, gentle, meaningful, and beneficial, out of compassion"—this is what the Blessed One has said; therefore, you are being told this.
If, while being praised, you remain steadfast in both freedom from anger and truthful speech, [you will attain success].

One should receive what is worth hearing, just as a person being bathed accepts the water. Having understood that my words are beneficial for this life and the next, act accordingly for your own welfare and for that of the world.

If, after having obtained wealth from supplicants in the past, you do not give it away out of ingratitude and greed, you will not obtain wealth again. In this world, even wholesome food does not sustain one who is not paid, though he may have been hired.
But the beggar, not being supported, becomes impoverished in the next world and carries a hundredfold debt.
One who possesses a noble mind should always delight in noble deeds;
for one whose actions are noble, every result that arises is noble.
"Build a glorious and renowned abode of Dharma, which has not even been touched by the feeble desires of kings, and which is the sanctuary of the Three Jewels—
that abode of Dharma which causes the hair on the bodies of neighboring kings to stand on end."
"O King, even death is not to be praised; therefore, it is better that this [act] be left undone.

Since it increases the wonder and enthusiasm of the noble through its extreme magnanimity, yet destroys the enthusiasm of the dull-witted, cause it to be performed even at the cost of your entire fortune. (RATNA_04.11-12)
Having abandoned everything here, you must go to the next world powerless;
yet all that which was dedicated to Dharma goes before you.
All the property of a former king falls under the control of the current king.

Is it for the sake of former merit, for happiness, or even for fame? (RATNA_04.14) In this world, happiness comes from wealth that has been enjoyed; happiness in the next world comes from what has been given.
Since there is no enjoyment and what was not given is lost, there is only suffering—how could there be happiness? (RATNA_04.15)

As you perish, you will be unable to give away [your wealth] because of your lack of independence, owing to ministers who are devoid of affection due to the destruction of their own interests and who seek only to please the new king.
Therefore, while you are still healthy, quickly establish a foundation for the Dharma even with all your possessions.
Standing amidst the conditions of death like a lamp in a gale;
and as for those other matters concerning the Dharma previously established by former kings,
such as the temple precincts and so forth, let them also continue to function as they were.
They should be served by those who are non-violent, of virtuous conduct, established in their vows, fond of guests, all-forgiving, free from quarrels, and ever-exerting;
as well as by the blind, the diseased, the deformed, the wretched, the helpless, and beggars.
May they also receive food and drink in moderation, without obstruction.
Grant appropriate favors even to those righteous people who are not seeking anything,
even if they reside in other kingdoms.
In all matters concerning the Dharma, appoint a Dharma-official who is upright,
free from greed, wise, righteous, and one who does not obstruct them;
[appoint those who] are knowledgeable in policy, virtuous, affectionate, pure, devoted, and undaunted.
Appoint as ministers those of noble lineage, endowed with virtuous conduct, and grateful.
Appoint as commanders of the army those who are not mean-spirited, generous, brave, affectionate, capable of sharing in prosperity, steadfast, ever-vigilant, and righteous.
Appoint as officials those who are virtuous in character, pure, capable, knowledgeable in their duties, experts in the treatises,
established in their livelihoods, impartial, affectionate, and elderly; and every month, you should hear from them the full account of all income and expenditure.
Having heard this, speak yourself regarding all matters concerning the administration of justice:
"If your kingdom is for the sake of Dharma, and not for the sake of fame or sensual pleasure, then it is exceedingly fruitful; otherwise, it serves no purpose."
O King, since this world has for the most part become a prey to one another,
listen to how your kingdom and your righteousness may both flourish.
[Let there be] those born of noble lineage, advanced in knowledge, conversant with justice, and fearful of sin.
May many who observe your affairs always be assembled together.
Even if they should inflict punishments, imprisonment, blows, and the like according to the law,
may you always remain moist with compassion and be full of grace toward them.
O King, you should always uplift the minds of all embodied beings for their very benefit out of compassion— even toward those who commit grave evils. Indeed,
one must especially exercise compassion toward those who are violent and have committed heinous crimes.
For they alone, being free from pride, are the objects of compassion for the great-souled ones.
Every day, or every five nights, release those who are bound and exhausted;
release the rest as well according to what is appropriate, but do not fail to release anyone at all.
In those [beings] toward whom the thought of not liberating them arises, there is non-restraint;
from that non-restraint, evil is accumulated incessantly.
And as long as they are not liberated, they remain bound by suffering.
Provided with shaves, baths, drinks, food, medicine, and clothing,
one should administer a beating out of compassion toward sons who are like unworthy vessels, desiring only to make them worthy vessels— not out of hatred, nor from a desire for gain.
Having reflected thoroughly and having correctly discerned those who are corrupt and even murderers,
banish those men from the realm without killing them and without causing them pain.
Being independent, survey the entire realm with the eyes of your spies.
Always heedful and mindful, perform your duties in accordance with the Dharma.
Constantly honor those established in virtue with gifts, respect, and hospitality;
likewise, according to the rules, treat the rest with noble and appropriate conduct.

The royal tree— its flowers in full bloom through proper honor, its great fruit being generosity, and its shade being forbearance— is resorted to by those who look to their livelihood. A king composed of the virtues of renunciation and moral conduct becomes beloved when he possesses splendor.
Just as a sugar-candy is roughened by cardamom and black pepper,
so too your kingdom will not exist through the "law of the fish" (the rule of the strong);
there will be neither injustice nor unrighteousness, but rather righteousness itself will prevail.
"You did not bring this kingdom from the next world, nor will you take it there;

since it was obtained through righteousness (*dharma*), you ought not to commit unrighteousness for its sake. Do not, for the sake of a kingdom—the price of a commodity—[exchange it] for a succession of commodities that are suffering."

O King, exert such effort as you may so that you do not fail to acquire [merit]. O King, exert such effort as you may so that you enjoy the succession of royal treasures by means of the kingdom itself as the price for those treasures.
Even for a universal monarch who has obtained the earth with its four continents,
these two kinds of happiness— bodily and mental—
are considered to be merely the counteraction of suffering; bodily pleasant feeling is nothing more than a remedy for pain.
But that which consists of perception is merely mental, produced solely by conceptual construction.
It is merely a remedy for suffering and nothing more than a conceptual construct;
therefore, this entire "wealth of happiness" for the world is, in reality, useless.
Islands, countries, cities, dwellings, regions, mountain slopes, and residences;
beds, food, drink, elephants, horses, and women—each of these is for the enjoyment of only one person.
And when the mind is directed toward any of these at any time, it is said that pleasure arises from them.
Because there is no mental attention (*amanaskāra*) toward the remaining [objects], those [other sensations] are in fact purposeless.
When one perceives objects with the five sense faculties, such as the eye,
and does not conceptualize them, there is no pleasure in them at that time.
Whichever object one perceives by whichever sense-organ,

at that time the remaining objects are not perceived by the remaining organs, since they would otherwise be useless at that moment. The mind [perceives] the form of the object apprehended by the sense-organs.
Having perceived [an object] that has passed away, one imagines it and conceives it as pleasure.
(RATNA_04.53) Even though a single sense-faculty here cognizes a single object, that faculty is useless without the object, and the object is likewise useless without it. (RATNA_04.54)
Just as the birth of a son is said to occur in dependence upon the mother and father,
so too is the arising of consciousness said to occur in dependence upon the eye and visible form.
Past and future objects, along with the sense faculties, are devoid of efficacy.
Since they do not exist apart from those two, even those things which are considered "present" are useless.
Just as the eye perceives a circle of fire due to a visual error,
so too do the sense faculties perceive objects as if they were present.
The sense faculties and the objects of the sense faculties are considered to be composed of the five elements;
since each element would be redundant on its own, these [faculties and objects] are in fact devoid of reality.
If the elements were distinct from one another, it would follow that fire could exist without fuel.
In contact there is an absence of characteristics; this is the conclusion regarding the remaining [elements] as well.
Thus, since the elements are useless in both ways, their conjunction is in vain.
And because conjunction is thus useless, form is therefore useless in reality.
And because the self is individually useless for consciousness, sensation, perception, and mental formations in every respect, they are ultimately useless from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Just as the conceit of pleasure regarding suffering is [merely] a remedy for it in reality, so too is this [conceit of self].

Likewise, even the conceit of suffering arises from the obstruction of pleasure. Thus, through the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), craving for union with pleasure is abandoned; and craving for separation from suffering is likewise abandoned for those who see this—therefore, liberation belongs to them.
If it is asked, "Who sees?", it is said, by way of conventional usage, that it is the mind (*citta*).
For a mind cannot exist without mental factors (*caitta*); since [the latter] would otherwise be purposeless, they are not admitted [to be non-existent].
Having thus understood the world to be purposeless according to reality, one becomes free from any basis for attachment.
Just as a fire without fuel goes out for lack of fuel,
so too the Bodhisattva, having seen this, is considered destined for perfect enlightenment;
yet, solely due to his compassion, his continuity of existence persists until that enlightenment.
The equipment of a bodhisattva has been taught by the Tathāgatas in the Mahāyāna;
yet it is reviled by those who are utterly deluded and by those who are full of hatred.
Either they are ignorant of virtues and faults, or they perceive faults where there are virtues.
Alternatively, one who hates virtues and reviles the Mahāyāna—
having recognized that faults belong to those who harm others and virtues to those who benefit others— is called a hater of virtues and a reviler of the Mahāyāna.
Because it is indifferent to its own interest and delights solely in the welfare of others, that Mahāyāna is a mine of virtues; therefore, one who hates it is consumed by that very hatred.
Even a person of faith might feel hostility toward it through a wrong grasp, while another, being angry, would do so for other reasons.

It is said that even a faithful person is "burnt"; what wonder then regarding one who is an ally of hatred? Just as physicians have stated that poison may be used to destroy poison, why is there a contradiction in saying that even through suffering one may destroy what is harmful?

Since it is taught in the scriptures that "mental states are preceded by the mind; the mind is supreme," how could one who acts for the benefit of others with a beneficial mind perform what is harmful even through suffering?
Even suffering that is beneficial for the future must be undertaken, let alone happiness that is beneficial.
This is the eternal law for oneself and for others.
If, by relinquishing a small pleasure, a vast happiness follows later,
the wise person should renounce that small pleasure, foreseeing the vast happiness.
If one does not tolerate this [criticism], then those who provide bitter medicine—such as physicians and the like—would be destroyed; yet this is not at all reasonable.
Even that which is seen to be unwholesome is sometimes considered wholesome by the wise.
In all the scriptures, both general rules and exceptions are taught.
Since all the outflows therein are preceded by compassion and are purified by wisdom,
what conscious person would disparage that Mahāyāna?
Because of its extreme vastness and profound depth, the Mahāyāna is today reviled out of delusion by those of undisciplined mind who are despondent and who act as enemies to themselves and others.
It consists of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, and compassion.
Therefore, why would there be any ill-spoken word in that Mahāyāna?
Through generosity and ethical discipline, the welfare of others is achieved; through patience and vigor, one's own [welfare];
and through meditative concentration and wisdom, liberation—this is the summary of the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
In brief, the Buddha’s teaching is for the sake of the welfare and liberation of others;
it has the six perfections as its core, and therefore these words of the Buddha are such.
In this [teaching], the great path to awakening, consisting of merit and wisdom, was taught by the Buddhas.
That Mahāyāna has been taught; indeed, it is not seen because of ignorance.
Because his qualities are inconceivable like space, the Jina is said to possess inconceivable qualities;
since the majesty of the Buddha is found in the Mahāyāna, let this be accepted.
Even for the noble Śāradvatīputra, this is beyond the scope of mere ethical conduct;
since that majesty of the Buddha is inconceivable, why is it not accepted?
In the Mahāyāna, non-arising [is the truth], while for others, emptiness is destruction.
Since the identity of cessation and non-arising in their actual meaning must be accepted,
how could the teachings of the Mahāyāna and other [vehicles] not accord for the wise who thus perceive emptiness and the greatness of the Buddha through reasoning? (RATNA_04.86–87)

Because the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata with intentional meaning (*abhisandhi*) are difficult to understand, one should protect oneself through equanimity (*upekṣā*) regarding the statements that there is a single vehicle or three vehicles.
For through equanimity there is no demerit; from hatred comes evil, so how could there be merit?

Therefore, those who cherish themselves ought not to harbor hatred toward the Mahāyāna. Since neither the bodhisattva’s vow nor the dedication of practice is taught in the Śrāvaka-yāna, how could one become a bodhisattva through that?
The foundations for a bodhisattva’s awakening have not been taught by the Buddhas; nor is there any other authority in this matter—what one superior to the Jinas could there be?
[From that which is] endowed with the foundations, the meaning of the noble truths, and the factors of awakening.
By what means is the fruit of a Buddha superior to the path shared with the Śrāvakas?
The words spoken for the purpose of establishing one in the conduct of awakening were not spoken in the [Hīnayāna] Sūtras;
they were spoken in the Mahāyāna, and therefore they should be accepted by the wise.
Just as a grammarian might teach even the alphabet,
so did the Buddha teach the Dharma to those to be trained according to their capacity.
To some he taught the Dharma for the purpose of turning them away from evil deeds.
For some, it is for the sake of accomplishing merit; for some, it relies on duality; for others, it does not rely on duality. For some, it is profound and terrifying to the fearful;
for others, it is the means to achieve awakening, with emptiness and compassion as its essence.
Thus, the virtuous should eliminate all hostility toward the Mahāyāna;
rather, they should cultivate even greater faith for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment.
Through faith in the Mahāyāna and by practicing what it teaches, [one achieves this].
Supreme enlightenment is attained, as well as all intermediate happinesses;
the Dharma consisting of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and truth—especially for the householder—is said to have compassion as its core. Let that be firmly internalized.
Now, because of the world's contrary nature, governing according to Dharma is difficult;
therefore, for the sake of Dharma and fame, it is appropriate for you to apply yourself to its attainment.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "Instruction on Royal Conduct," from the *Ratnāvalī*.
